newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean voters send warning to president Kim.
newsitem.headline: South Korean voters send warning to president Kim.

text.p: South Korean voters handed crushing defeats to the ruling camp in two parliamentary by-elections in what political analysts described on Thursday as an ominous warning to President Kim Young-sam.

Wednesday's elections gave voters their first chance to pass judgement on Kim's use of sweeping government personnel changes to rehabilitate his image, sullied by a series of bribery scandals and political blunders.
On Wednesday, Kim reshuffled his cabinet, a day after naming a new prime minister.
Most worrying for Kim ahead of presidential polls, the by-elections showed the opposition was capable of uniting to trounce the ruling New Korea Party.

Although the two National Assembly seats in Suwon and Inchon were already held by the opposition, they were recaptured with thumping majorities after two main opposition groups joined forces behind a single candidate.
The result gave impetus to the National Congress for New Politics and United Liberal Democratic Party to forge a joint ticket to challenge for the presidency in December.
Kim is constitutionally barred from seeking a second term but is acting as kingmaker to try to install a protege.
In the previous two presidential elections, held every five years, the opposition failed to agree on a single candidate and split the vote, handing victory to the ruling camp.

"The opposition parties have been working on backing a single presidential candidate, and the by-election results give us confidence we could win," said Park Sung-suck, a spokeswoman for the National Congress.
Voters in Inchon and Suwon stayed away in droves, further highlighting the plight of the New Korea Party, which normally gains from a low turnout because it has a better-oiled political machine.
"The actual votes as well as the high abstention rate is a message of warning to President Kim Young-sam," said Kim Byung-kook, political science professor at Korea University.
Kim said unless the ruling camp improved its performance "the next presidential election will be the first where we will see an opposition candidate come to power".
The National Congress is led by veteran dissident Kim Dae-jung, who is widely believed to be preparing a fourth bid for the presidency.
There has been speculation Kim Dae-jung's candidacy would be opposed by Kim Jong-pil, an arch-conservative who heads the much smaller United Liberal party.

"If the opposition backs a single presidential candidate, they could win the elections this year, but if they don't, the ruling party would win regardless of all the scandals," said Seoul National University professor Lee Jung-bock.
The ruling party provoked almost four weeks of labour strikes after ramming through parliament a controversial new labour law last December.

It has also been badly wounded by a bribery scandal involving loans to the bankrupt Hanbo Steel Co. Three of Kim's closest New Korea Party aides are now in custody following a probe into the scandal, which demolished the president's reputation for fighting graft.
Lee said Suwon and Inchon voters had shown "discontent and mistrust" towards the government.
The two seats became vacant through deaths following general elections last April.

In Suwon, the United Liberal candidate captured 28,780 votes against 16,018 for his ruling party opponent. This compared with a winning margin of just 586 votes for the previous United Liberal incumbent.
In Inchon, the National Congress candidate trounced his New Korea Party adversary by 42,503 votes to 24,070.
